practice.title: Faith in Emptiness
agreedSteps: Maintain a mind of faith throughout daily life — during walks, conversations, at work, watching TV, at the doctor's office, getting yelled at, receiving scary news. Can I remember and hold faith in my heart in those moments?

Practice 'by words' — have a list of teachings or Buddha's words that we have faith in, that feel infallible or true. When a mind of non-faith or doubt arises, go through the list, reciting or remembering those exact words to interrupt the doubt.

Catch ourselves seeking just temporary liberations and notice the satisfaction — ah, that's better. Start to feel that temporary liberation is not enough. Faith in emptiness specifically is the center.
steps: Increase effort by increasing faith. Instead of hammering away at a practice hoping it makes a change, put energy into increasing faith in the practice and let that naturally flow downhill into effort — a much gentler way to practice.

When practicing, check: what's really the motivation? How often is it really for happiness of future lives, freedom from samsara, or to become a Buddha? Or is it just a sophisticated medication with very few side effects?
practice.quote: In a sense, our faith is really faith in emptiness. That's really our refuge. Buddha is awesome, but it's actually faith in emptiness. That's the only way to attain permanent liberation.

commentary.title: Two Causes of Going for Refuge
content: Going for refuge is a major foundation of the Buddhist path. It signifies our determination to turn away from the endless cycle of confusion and dissatisfaction that has marked our life, and towards a saner, more wholesome way of living.

There are two interrelated causes for taking refuge. First, a heartfelt dread of the miserable states of samsaric existence towards which our uncontrolled behavior is propelling us — an intense aversion to the sufferings of the lower realms, or a feeling of being disgusted with the unsatisfactory nature of all states conditioned by ignorance. Second, an unshakable conviction and faith in the Three Jewels, understanding how they have the power to protect us from all forms of suffering.

We can ask ourselves: what do I really think is the answer to the suffering of this world? Where do I go for refuge? We go to the police if we're fearful, to doctors if we're sick. Many people go for refuge to politics — which is completely bizarre, just trying to fix samsara. So we check: what do I think about all day? What do I put my energy into? When I'm fearful, unhappy, worried — where do I go for relief?

commentary.title: Three Scopes of Going for Refuge
content: At the initial level, a person sees how their mind is polluted by violent delusions and fears that without proper training, this unruly mind will expose them to the intense suffering of the lower realms. They develop faith in the Three Jewels to protect them. At the intermediate level, a person sees how all of samsaric existence is pervaded by suffering, and turns to the Three Jewels for a method to gain complete liberation. At the highest level, motivated by great compassion, the seeker transcends selfish concerns and turns to the Three Jewels with the conviction that only they can lead to enlightenment.

This points us directly at the Lamrim, which is designed to develop these three scopes — the initial scope is the first five meditations, the intermediate scope is the sixth, and the great scope is the twenty-first. Without cultivating these higher aims, which have to be quite deliberately trained in, we're not really on a spiritual path.

commentary.title: Faith Is Our Spiritual Life
content: For Buddhists, faith in Buddha Shakyamuni is their spiritual life. It is the root of all Dharma realizations. If we have deep faith, we naturally develop the strong wish to practice his teachings. This wish implies effort. With strong effort, we accomplish permanent liberation. The chain: faith → aspiration → effort → liberation. And in reverse: liberation depends on effort, effort depends on aspiration, aspiration depends on faith.

In a sense, the first thing to develop is faith in faith itself. We're admiring faith, believing in the power of faith, wishing to develop our faith. Why? Because it's the root of all spiritual attainments. We're not Buddha yet — so we can definitely increase it. Faith is not a byproduct or a passive thing. It's a mental factor, like compassion or wisdom. It's a state of mind that we cultivate very purposely.

commentary.title: Temporary Liberation Is Not Enough
content: To grow our faith, we need to repeatedly think about how temporary liberation is not good enough. All living beings experience temporary liberation — animals from human suffering, humans from animal suffering. But in samsara, no one has permanent liberation.

Temporary liberation is unsatisfactory in several ways. First, it's deceptive — it kind of works, and can make us miss the point. Oh, I don't need Dharma, everything is better now. Sometimes we should consider: what kind of temporary liberations could dupe me off my path? What if everything became wonderful and easy? Would I stop practicing? Second, we die. If we're not permanently liberated, some mess starts up — no guarantee of a precious human life or a spiritual path next time. Third, temporary liberations don't give us the ability to help other people. There's something selfish and hedonistic about temporary liberation.

A useful heuristic: if I need this temporary relief in order to get ultimate relief, it makes sense. Like a painkiller so I can think clearly enough to practice. But if it's just distraction, or I'm deluding myself that it IS the ultimate relief, it doesn't make sense. Even Dharma practice can become just a sophisticated medication if the intention is only comfort in the here and now.

commentary.title: Faith in Emptiness Specifically
content: The center of our faith is thinking: I have faith in Buddha specifically and above all because he teaches me emptiness. Our faith is really faith in emptiness. That's really our refuge. Why without emptiness specifically is it impossible to attain permanent liberation?

All suffering comes from delusions. You can't get rid of delusions — especially attachment and aversion — without realizing emptiness. What would it be like to have no attachment at all? It's almost unfathomable without imagining a realization of emptiness. Even in the highest god realm of pure bliss, there would still be attachment settling in. And as long as there's an I imputed on an ordinary body and mind, that in itself is pervasive suffering, no matter how good things are. That can only stop through emptiness.

Only Buddhist teachings are the actual methods to abandon self-grasping ignorance. As Buddha says in The King of Concentration Sutra: 'A magician creates various things such as horses, elephants, and so forth. His creations do not actually exist. You should know all things in the same way.' This teaching alone has the power to permanently liberate all living beings.

commentary.title: The Three Jewels Are About Emptiness
content: From Joyful Path, the Dharma Jewel is defined as: a perfectly purified truth in the continuum of a superior being. The actual Dharma Jewel is true cessations and true paths. A true cessation is permanent because it is the emptiness of a mind that has attained complete abandonment of any obstruction. It is not merely the final abandonment of a delusion — it is the emptiness of a mind that has attained such a cessation. This is why liberation can't end: true cessations are permanent because they are emptiness.

The Sangha Jewel is a superior being who has realized emptiness directly. The Buddha Jewel is the ultimate source of refuge — non-produced, effortlessly attained, free from all faults. Non-produced refers to the true cessations that are the abandonment of both delusion obstructions and obstructions to omniscience. Since these are permanent, they are called non-produced.

So the Dharma Jewel of emptiness is our object of faith in Dharma. The Sangha Jewel — people who realize emptiness — is our faith in Sangha. And Buddha, who is one with emptiness and reveals emptiness, is why we have faith in Buddha. Over time we want to keep upgrading our understanding of these definitions, not just have it stay where it's been for a few years.

commentary.title: Blessings Are a Necessary Cause
content: By themselves, living beings are unable to cultivate a peaceful mind. A blessing is actually a 100% required contributory cause for a virtuous mind to arise — like moisture is required for a cloud. Without it, a virtuous mind is simply not on the table.

When we're receiving a blessing, we're actually connecting with the truth. That's all a blessing is. And without connecting with the truth, we're not going to get a peaceful mind. The self on its own is a closed loop — completely self-referential, which is basically non-existent. You can't do anything on your own. Walk, talk, breathe, exist on your own. It always has to be in relationship to something else.

The word 'blessing' means to transform — for our mind to transform from an ego state to a positive state. It's implying that on its own, the mind can't make that transformation. It needs another influence.

commentary.title: Memorizing Buddha's Speech — Rocket Ship vs. Skateboard
content: Buddha's speech is blessed — it's basically Buddha's mind appearing as speech. So memorizing a verse or passage and then wielding it actively is a very powerful practice. It's much more powerful than thinking through something in our own way. It's like a huge blazing rocket ship compared to a little skateboard. Because we're calling on Buddha's mind when we memorize Buddha's speech and recite it with faith — we're accessing a Buddha's mind, versus just trying to think through our problems in our normal way.

This is a great practical tool: memorize a verse that speaks to our particular challenge, and wield it when the challenge arises. Recite it hundreds of times if needed. The shift comes from going to our faith and connecting to Buddha's mind, not from a cognitive analytical solution.
